extracted.intended_audience: diplomats and treaty negotiators drafting consular conventions (U.S.–France) and government legal advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and specific suggested alterations for articles of a consular convention between the United States and France, addressing immunities, jurisdiction, evidence, arrest powers, language/authenticity, and duration. Intended to inform treaty drafting and negotiation to align the instrument with U.S. law and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular immunities (article 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth article gives to the consuls the immunities of the law of nations; it has been understood that the laws of France do not admit of this; and that it might be desirable to expunge this article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an article confers immunities that conflict with the domestic law of the receiving state, the U.S. is ready to concur in expunging it. Do not agree to broad immunity provisions that cannot be executed under U.S. legal principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations by consuls 'in their own houses' (article 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth article requires, after certain formalities, that declarations be made 'in their own houses' (chez eux), implying that consuls need not submit to personal examination before courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. law requires personal examination of witnesses in the presence of parties, counsel, jury, and judge; therefore omit any clause that permits testimony only 'in their own houses.' If article 4 is removed, article 5 (an exception) becomes moot and should be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular certificates as conclusive evidence (articles 7, 8, 10, 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some articles require that declarations certified by consuls be received in evidence in all courts whatever and, in some instances, give certificates credibility which excludes all other testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. practice rarely admits written evidence of facts, and when admitted it must be given in the presence of both parties with answers to all pertinent questions. Do not accept provisions that make consular certificates conclusive and exclude counter-proof; permit courts to receive counter-evidence and preserve established evidentiary safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of consular jurisdiction over other foreigners (article 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: The eighth article gives to the consuls of either nation jurisdiction, in certain cases, over foreigners of any other nationality (e.g., an American consul deciding disputes between an American and a Spaniard or Englishman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial judges are neutral and more impartial in disputes involving third nationals; correct or limit any provision granting consuls jurisdiction over non-nationals to avoid unfairly abandoning third parties to a foreign consul's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular jurisdiction between two subjects of the same foreign state (article 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The twelfth article gives jurisdiction to a consul in disputes arising between two subjects of the same foreign state when one is in the other country (e.g., dispute between two French subjects with one in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the territorial tribunals of the country where the dispute arises; do not cede jurisdiction to foreign consuls in cases properly within domestic courts' competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to arrest and send back vessels, captains, crews (article 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tenth article grants power of arrest and sending back a vessel, its captain, and crew — a very great authority over persons and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such high-handed powers are more safely lodged with the territorial judge (or admiralty courts), which are neutral and legally trained; reserve this power to domestic admiralty courts rather than to single consuls, except where narrowly needed and clearly defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest of deserted seamen vs. passengers (article 10 distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrest and detention of deserted seamen is considered necessary for navigation and commerce and may be entrusted to consuls; arrest/detention of passengers is unnecessary for navigation/commerce and not within consul functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow consuls authority to arrest deserted seamen for practical navigation/commercial reasons, but prohibit extension of arrest powers to passengers, as this may conflict with fundamental rights (bills of rights) and exceed consular functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistance of territorial judge to consul in exercising arrest powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 10 requires the territorial judge to assist the consul in the exercise of arrest powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer leaving arrest and detention powers to territorial judges or admiralty courts; assent may be given only where assistance is necessary for specific consular functions (e.g., deserted seamen), but avoid provisions that broadly obligate domestic judges to execute consular authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit convention duration (probationary clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consular institutions being new with the U.S., Congress thinks it wise to make the first convention probationary, not perpetual; propose a clause limiting its duration to a certain term of years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a fixed-term or sunset clause so each party can assess experience and renew or amend the convention later; promote flexibility and avoid permanent commitments before practical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilingual equally-authentic texts
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention, as expressed in French, will answer purposes in France, but not in America; translations may misrender legal/technical terms. Propose the convention be faithfully expressed in English as well as French, in two columns, each declared text to be equally original and authentic in courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and publish the instrument in both languages side-by-side and declare both texts authentic to avoid disputes over meaning caused by imperfect translations; ensure drafters set equivalents for legal/technical phrases at formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid articles incompatible with domestic legal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Some articles, in their present form, could not be executed at all under our laws; others would produce embarrassments and ill humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not agree to treaty provisions that domestic law cannot implement; prefer fewer, practicable articles that will be observed rather than many idealistic ones that cannot be executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consular privileges to avoid jealousy and reciprocity issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending consular privileges and jurisdictions too far may render them objects of jealousy and irritation in places of residence; treaties with other nations will invite claims for privileges granted to any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise circumspection in granting privileges; avoid concessions that will obligate similar privileges to other nations by reciprocity or provoke local resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consuls' primary functions: navigation and commerce only
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution of consuls is for the objects of navigation and commerce only; functions beyond those (e.g., wide judicial powers) are not appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict consular functions to commerce/navigation matters; do not expand into broad judicial or police powers inconsistent with the consul’s commercial role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical preference for commercial correspondents over consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mercantile house has correspondents in almost every port; correspondents take better care of merchants' interests and obtain protection more effectively than consuls, who are generally foreigners unpossessed of useful local details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that private commercial correspondents often provide better practical protection and assistance to merchants than consuls; avoid structuring conventions based on overvaluing consular role where commercial networks serve the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation/publication risk: congressional translation liability
rubrics_metrics.description: If any translation published by Congress does not fully render the idea of the French original, it might be imputed as an indirect attempt to abridge or extend a contract at the will of one party only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent post-facto translation disputes by preparing both authentic texts at the time of drafting; do not rely on a unilateral later translation which could be challenged as altering terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft fewer, well-observed articles rather than many
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer articles, better observed, will better promote common interests; an instrument intended to strengthen connection might become the means of loosening it if ill-drafted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise, workable provisions that can be implemented and respected; prioritize clarity and enforceability over breadth of concessions.
